title: NMR console: the analog front end and its housing
blurb: Work in progress. The analog side of the class board - thirteen nets from the link header out to the SMA field and the TX coil terminal - routed with no vias at all, so no analog signal changes reference plane. Around it a printed housing measured from the board meshes, its cover at two heights so an SMA thread stands 5.5 mm proud while a raised box clears the 13.8 mm OLED.

title: Benchtop NMR instrument
blurb: A 2 mT NMR instrument around the class board: housing, probe, B0 coils, fabrication files and an interactive bench simulator. Design stage: nothing built or measured yet, all data simulated. The project site has the whole story.

title: iPhone 16 Pro Max case
blurb: A parametric phone case, written in OpenSCAD with BOSL2 after the housing, to see whether the same approach transfers. Only the body - 163.0 x 77.6 x 8.25 mm - could be verified from Apple's specs; the corner radius, camera island and every button position are estimates, each marked MEASURE in the file. For TPU, not PLA: a case has to stretch to go on and come off.

title: iPad Air 5 stand
blurb: Two viewing angles, printed flat on its side so the whole part is one constant cross-section and nothing overhangs. The first version had notch positions from a formula with an invented constant in it, and the top notch broke out through the spine. It now checks each slot tip against the top edge.

title: Three-electrode cell lid
blurb: For the electrochemistry side of my own research. Uncompensated resistance is whatever sits between the working electrode and the reference tip, so a cell clamped by hand has a different one every setup. Drawing it found a conflict: a 6 mm reference cannot sit 5 mm from a 6 mm working electrode - the holes merge. That is what a Luggin capillary is for.

title: Spin Echo
blurb: A timing game whose mechanic is the physics rather than a skin over it. A 90 degree pulse fires; you fire the 180. Dephasing is the spins losing agreement, not energy, so a pulse can undo it - but each shot hides its own T2, which nothing can, and the echo lands at twice your delay. Fire early and there is nothing to recover; late and T2 has eaten it.

title: Screw-cap pencil tube
blurb: A drawing-tube in miniature: M44 x 4 coarse thread, four turns to close. Coarse because fine does not print - the flanks of an M44x1.5 are two extrusions wide at a 0.4 mm nozzle and the cap binds. THREAD_SLOP is the only fit in the part and the one thing a printer's tolerance moves.

title: NMR receive coil former
blurb: The receiver's noise budget rests on one number: 2.53 mH sets the resonating capacitor, the tank resistance and so the 15.3 nV/rtHz floor. Hand-wind twice and none of it describes the bench. A 38.5 x 2.7 mm winding window gives 546 turns and 2.52 mH. A single layer cannot reach it - 2900 turns, 1.2 m long.

title: Class board instrument: the housing
blurb: The class board, a small instrument and NMR console on an ESP32-S3, in a printed housing: a base, a two-colour labelled cover, a separate SMA plate and an OLED hood, closed by a laser-cut acrylic lid. Every dimension came from the KiCad files and board meshes, and a clash test of all three board models against every part came back clean.

title: Slingshot
blurb: Drag back from the probe and let go; everything after that is Newtonian gravity and nothing else, for seven levels. The last level is provably impossible on your own - the furthest any launch can reach is r = 1006 against a ring at 1150, by analysis and by brute force alike - so you have to steal speed from a passing moon.

title: Pixel Plumber
blurb: The first game I built for this course: a Mario-style platformer that runs on a phone, with touch controls, coins, goombas and a flag at the end. It later grew low-gravity and no-friction zones with a live physics readout, and that is where I learned the physics has to change how the game plays, not just what the screen reports.

title: Mario Classic
blurb: The original Mario-style platformer from this repository, preserved exactly as it was first committed in a147605: touch controls, coins, goombas and a flag at the end, on constant gravity with no physics extras. The later version added low-gravity and no-friction zones and a live readout; this is the game before any of that, and the three files are byte-identical to that commit.

title: Echo Bridge: The Last Ferry
blurb: A six-chapter platform adventure: reverse moving bridges, deliver a toolbox, and help a harbor catch the last ferry. Every chapter has a verified playable route; optional notes connect your own crossing to NMR phase refocusing.

title: Photon Bench
blurb: Place 45-degree mirrors on an optical breadboard to steer 638, 589, 532 and 447 nm beams past beam dumps and through dichroic gates into the photodiode that matches their wavelength. Seven stages; the surprise is the last one, where two beams have to cross the same empty square and pass clean through each other.

title: Calculator
blurb: A clean browser calculator with standard arithmetic, keyboard support, and a modern dark UI. It demonstrates a small but polished front-end build that works well on desktop and mobile without extra libraries.

title: Unfair Golf
blurb: An 8-hole browser golf game where every hole breaks a different rule of physics instead of just adding a hazard: gusting wind, a near-frictionless green, an inverse-square gravity well, teleporter pads, a drifting cup, and mirrored controls. Every wall bounce also carries randomized restitution, so no rebound is ever quite predictable.

title: Glowmeter
blurb: A phone web app that sets an ESP32-S3's onboard LED (colour + brightness) and streams a live measurement back as a strip chart at 20 Hz, over one WebSocket, no server in between. Runs unmodified class-board-2026 firmware; only the phone app is new, and it's flashed onto the board's own filesystem so it's served locally, avoiding any HTTPS/WebSocket mixed-content issue.

title: Load the train
blurb: Drive a locomotive and twenty hopper cars under a grain chute and fill them without spilling: grain leaves the chute with no forward speed, so every tonne you load drags the train back, harder the faster you go. The surprise is that the locomotive can outrun its own chute — full power settles at 6.2 m/s, but a car only reaches 90 % in one pass below 4.8 m/s.

title: Cart-pole — the reference example
blurb: The instructor's reference for a Project-1 build: a cart-pole you push with the arrow keys, or leave to a PD controller to balance. It exists to show a simulation being checked — predicted 2π√(L/g) = 2.006 s against 1.987 s measured, with the cart recoil and the finite amplitude accounting for the difference to 0.1 %.
